This chapter covers cybernetic augmentation — acquisition, installation and medical risk, neural and sensory implants, and cybernetic prosthetics — along with the universal item condition and degradation system used for all equipment types.

During the Mandalorian Wars, medical technology has advanced to the point where the organic body can be seamlessly integrated with cybernetic enhancements. These upgrades range from life-saving prosthetic limbs to military-grade neural processors. However, in this war-torn era, technology is often utilitarian and gritty. Cybernetic installations are clinical, invasive, and carry inherent mechanical vulnerabilities.

Note: Weight of implants and cybernetics only apply to a character’s total weight carried when not installed to the user, and in their inventory. Cybernetics and Implants of any kind are not compatible with droid characters.

Whether a character acquires a new cybernetic implant or limb during character creation, or the campaign, they pay the Credit (CR) cost of the part. In both cases the player must add the Mandatory Traits for having a cybernetic for first time installers.

  • The Trait Package: The player must spend CP on the specific Advantages granted by the cybernetic (e.g., Arm ST, Extra Arms, Damage Resistance, Telescopic Vision).
  • Mandatory Flaws: To balance this, the character must take the Disadvantages, Limitations, and Quirks inherent to possessing mechanical hardware. This includes the mandatory limitations like Electrical (-20 points) and Daily Maintenance (-10 points), as well as optional physical flaws like Unhealing (Partial or Total), or Numb. The points returned from these flaws offset the cost of the advantages. The CP column in this chapter’s tables is the total those granted Advantages come to, and nothing more. It is not a separate price the character pays on top of them, it is not net of the Mandatory Flaws above, and a replacement of hardware the character already has costs no CP at all (see Replacing Existing Cybernetics, below). Read it as a working figure for building the Trait Package, never as the implant’s cost in points.

During the campaign, if a character is replacing a cybernetic they already possess—such as swapping a heavily damaged Combat-Grade arm for a new one of the exact same type—they do not need to spend Character Points again on the Mandatory Traits.

  • Credit (CR) Cost Only: The character only needs to pay the in-game economic cost. This means paying the CR value for the replacement hardware and the surgeon’s fee.
  • Medical Recovery: The character must undergo the standard downtime (defined under Time, the Calendar, and Downtime, @UUID[Compendium.shadowbase.handbook.JournalEntry.SQjNPFSBwLhhCFQ2]{Chapter 20}), deal with the after-effects of the surgery, and risk the potential complications of the procedure (e.g., tissue rejection or temporary stat penalties on a failed Surgery roll).

Cybernetics in this era are highly invasive and clinical. Surgical installation is a mandatory requirement for all cybernetics and implants, not just neural ones. Whether a character is getting a brand-new implant or simply replacing a destroyed mechanical hand, the procedure requires professional medical intervention, a sterile operating environment, and dedicated recovery time.

Every piece of hardware, whether a prosthetic limb or a cognitive booster, must have the following limitations applied to its base point cost:

  • Electrical (-20 points): Internal cybernetic components are vulnerable to high-voltage surges. EMP and Ion attacks deal structural deactivation, potentially shutting down or damaging components.
  • Daily Maintenance (-10 points): A mundane physical Disadvantage where character requires skilled attention daily to avoid HT loss. Skipping a daily maintenance period causes the subject to immediately lose 1 point of HT (Health), and requires them to roll against their newly reduced HT to avoid any further losses.

When a player creates a character with a cybernetic body part, or an implant, they must calculate the Character Point cost systematically. This process ensures that whether the character is replacing a lost arm or adding a third arm to their torso, the costs are balanced.

Follow these steps to determine the final Character Point cost of any cybernetic limb or implant.

Step 1: Determine the Base Limb Status First, determine if the cybernetic part is replacing a standard humanoid limb or if it is an extra appendage.

  • Replacements: If the cybernetic limb replaces a standard natural limb, such as a character starting with a mechanical arm instead of a flesh one, they must pay the Credit cost of the limb alongside the mandatory traits.
  • Extra Limbs: If the player is adding extra limbs beyond the standard humanoid layout, they must purchase the base advantage for that limb. An Extra Arm costs 10 Character Points. An Extra Leg costs 5 Character Points. Extra Limbs introduce new hit locations to the character. Extra arms or legs are targeted by enemies at a -2 penalty, while extra hands or feet are targeted at a -4 penalty.

For more info on Hit Locations, see the Hit Locations section of @UUID[Compendium.shadowbase.handbook.JournalEntry.JJ04T5LHImjlILs1]{Chapter 7}.*

Step 2: Add Augmentations and Advantages Next, add the Character Point cost of any internal augmentations, such as Arm Strength, built-in weapon mounts, or Super Jump capabilities. The base Character Point costs for these common traits are listed in the Common Advantages section below. For neural or sensory implants that do not require an entire limb replacement, you simply start at this step and sum the cost of the traits the implant provides.

Step 3: Apply System Limitations Take the combined total Character Point sum and apply the Mandatory Cybernetic Traits.

Whether splicing an advanced neural processor directly into the brain stem, embedding tactical HUD optics in the skull, or replacing a shattered arm with military-grade alloy, all cybernetic installations are major, invasive surgical procedures. They cannot be swapped out or installed in the field.

The Surgical Process

  • The Surgeon: The procedure requires a successful Surgery skill roll by an attending physician. In the absence of a proper surgeon, the procedure can be attempted at a default penalty using First Aid-12, Physician-5, Physiology-8, or Veterinary-5 (typical of back-alley doctors, or emergency battlefield triage). A character can perform the surgery on themselves only if they possess the Surgery skill and have access to a fully automated medical bay.
  • Surgical Costs: The player must pay the cost of surgery each time an implant or limb is installed or removed. This cost is variable depending on the quality of the clinic and the legality of the tech, but typically ranges between 1,000 to 5,000 Credits.
  • Time & Recovery: The surgical procedure takes several hours of intensive operating time.

Installation Complications & Risks

On a failed Surgery roll, the medical procedure succeeds but the hardware is poorly calibrated. The user suffers localized physical setbacks, and the cybernetic’s active bonuses remain offline until a surgeon successfully recalibrates it. On a critical failure, the patient suffers severe bodily trauma and the hardware is permanently ruined.

These risks are specialized by technology category:

1. Neural Implants (Brain Stem & Central Nervous System)

  • Failure (Poor Calibration): The body fights the deep biochemical and electrical shift. The user suffers a -1 penalty to DX and IQ for 1d days. The implant’s active bonuses are offline.
  • Critical Failure (Neural Shock): The patient takes 3d injury (bypassing DR), and the delicate neural implant is completely destroyed.

2. Sensory & Utility Implants (Eyes, Ears, Internal Organs)

  • Failure (Feedback Loop): The user suffers from visual static, high-pitched audio feedback, or equilibrium issues. This imposes a -1 penalty to Perception and a -2 penalty to HT rolls against sensory overload (such as flashbangs or sonic weapons) for 1d days. The implant’s active bonuses are offline.
  • Critical Failure (Sensory Trauma): The patient takes 2d injury (bypassing DR), the implant is destroyed, and they suffer from the Blindness or Deafness disadvantage (or Bad Sight / Hard of Hearing if only one of a pair of sensory organs was targeted) for 1d weeks due to nerve damage.

3. Prosthetics & Cybernetic Limbs (Arms, Legs, Extremities)

  • Failure (Tissue Rejection & Bad Fit): The biological stump or socket rejects the physical housing. The user suffers a -1 penalty to HT for 1d days, and faces an additional -1 penalty to physical skills utilizing that specific limb (e.g., Acrobatics for a leg, Lockpicking or Weapon skills for an arm). The limb’s built-in combat-grade bonuses are offline.
  • Critical Failure (Amputation / Structural Collapse): Severe arterial damage and infection at the graft point. The patient takes 3d injury (bypassing DR), the prosthetic limb is ruined (reduced to 0 DR and destroyed), and they gain the Chronic Pain (Mild) disadvantage for 1d weeks.

Because invasive surgical installation is a universal requirement for all hardware across the board, the foundational modifiers apply to everything, while specific physical and digital vulnerabilities split based on the nature of the technology.

Implants (Neural, Sensory, & Cognitive)

For internal systems that interface directly with the brain or nervous system, the focus shifts to digital vulnerabilities and neurological feedback.

Mandatory Disadvantages

  • Susceptibility (Computer Viruses/Malware): Neural implants are inherently vulnerable to electronic warfare. The character must take at least one level of this disadvantage, applying a penalty to resist digital hacking or localized malware.

Mandatory Quirks (Choose One)

  • Static Feedback (-1 point): Your neural interface occasionally suffers from micro-static when you get startled, causing you to briefly blink or rub your eyes.
  • Glitchy HUD (-1 point): Your sensory optical overlay occasionally shows flickering pixels or obsolete warning signs, which you stubbornly refuse to calibrate.
  • Dull (-1 point): You have very little imagination and a strictly literal, pragmatic view of the world, often leaning on the logical, algorithmic processing of your neural implants over emotional responses.

Cybernetics (Limbs & Structural Replacements)

For physical body replacements, the focus is on mechanical wear and tear, as well as the obvious physical differences from biological flesh.

Mandatory Disadvantages

  • Unhealing (Partial) (-20 points): Your biological flesh heals normally, but any cybernetic limbs and implants must be manually repaired using mechanical skills and materials.

Mandatory Quirks (Choose One)

  • Obsessive Overclocking (-1 point): You have a habit of compulsively optimizing your cooling and processing speeds whenever you have a quiet moment, sometimes causing minor whirring noises.
  • Tech Scavenger (-1 point): You have a habit of compulsively stripping downed droids, broken equipment, or abandoned consoles for spare parts, convinced they might be useful later to patch or upgrade your cybernetics.
  • Careful (-1 point): You are meticulous and cautious, often double-checking your cybernetic gear and calibrations. This is a deep-seated need for mechanical preparedness.

Before applying modifiers, these are the base costs for traits commonly integrated into a cybernetically enhanced character.

Physical & Combat Augmentations

  • Damage Resistance (DR) (5 CP / level): Subdermal armor plating or reinforced bone weaving.
  • Striking ST (5 CP / level): Hydraulic actuators or synthetic muscle fibers in an arm or hand. Adds only to damage, not lifting.
  • Lifting ST (3 CP / level): Reinforced joints and power-assist skeletal frameworks. Adds to carrying capacity, not striking damage.
  • Arm ST (3 CP per arm / level, or 5 CP for both arms / level): Enhances both lifting and striking strength specifically in the designated cybernetic limbs. The lifting it enhances is what those limbs do on their own -- arm wrestling, a one-armed haul, holding a weight out at arm's length -- and not your Basic Lift or carrying capacity, which run off ST and Lifting ST alone (@UUID[Compendium.shadowbase.handbook.JournalEntry.fZowiGenjFSpf9el]{Chapter 2}). The scope is identical to the natural version; only the rate differs.
  • Extra Arms (10 CP per arm): Fully functional, additional mechanical limbs mounted to the torso or shoulders.
  • Ambidexterity (5 CP): Neural recalibration allows the user to operate dual cybernetic arms with perfect synchronicity. No off-hand penalty in combat -- neither the -4 to hit nor the -1 to parry (@UUID[Compendium.shadowbase.handbook.JournalEntry.JJ04T5LHImjlILs1]{Chapter 7}). This is the cybernetic route to the same 5-point benefit as natural Ambidexterity; take whichever matches your hands, never both.
  • High Pain Threshold (10 CP): Pain receptors in cybernetic limbs are bypassed, allowing the user to shrug off physical trauma.
  • Combat Reflexes (15 CP): A hardwired tactical reflex processor. Grants +1 to active defenses, +2 to Fright Checks, and +6 to recover from mental stun.
  • Enhanced Time Sense (45 CP): A top-tier neural booster. Act first in combat, receive active defense bonuses against high-speed projectiles, and perceive the world in slow motion.
  • Super Jump (10 CP / level): Pneumatic pistons or kinetic thrusters built into the legs. Doubles jumping distance per level.
  • Innate Attack (Melee/Blades) (Approx. 2 to 5 CP / level): Retractable monofilament blades, forearm spurs, or shock claws built into the hands or arms.
  • Innate Attack (Ranged/Laser) (Approx. 5 to 8 CP / level): Integrated weaponry, such as a forearm laser or a palm-mounted kinetic ejector.

Sensory & Utility Implants

  • 360-Degree Vision (25 CP): Panoramic optic bands or auxiliary micro-cameras embedded around the skull. Every facing arc counts as Front: full active defense in all six hexes, never Flanked, and no facing change is needed to attack in any direction (see Facing, @UUID[Compendium.shadowbase.handbook.JournalEntry.JJ04T5LHImjlILs1]{Chapter 7}).
  • Infravision (0 CP or 10 CP): Thermal imaging. Costs 0 CP if replacing normal vision entirely, or 10 CP to have it as a switchable overlay.
  • Ultravision (0 CP or 10 CP): Ultraviolet light receptors. Costs 0 CP if replacing normal vision entirely, or 10 CP as an overlay.
  • Spectrum Vision (25 CP): Advanced multispectral optics (infrared, ultraviolet, X-rays, and electromagnetic radiation).
  • Telescopic Vision (5 CP / level): High-performance zoom lenses. Grants +1 per level to hit when taking an Aim turn.
  • Protected Senses (Vision or Hearing) (5 CP each): Automated optical shutters or audio dampening software. Immune to blinding flashes and deafening noises.
  • Absolute Direction (5 CP or 10 CP): Gyro-compass and GPS receiver. Grants +3 to Navigation. The 10 CP level includes 3D spatial mapping.
  • Absolute Timing (2 CP): An internal atomic clock synchronized with global network frequencies.
  • Temperature Tolerance (1 CP / level): Synthetic skin, coolant lines, and internal heaters.
  • Doesn’t Breathe (20 CP): Fully mechanical lungs or advanced blood-oxygen scrubbers.
  • Filter Lungs (5 CP): Internal chemical filters protecting against inhaled toxins, gases, and pathogens.
  • Telecommunication (Radio) (10 CP): An internal, subvocal radio transceiver.

Cognitive & Software Systems

  • Modular Abilities (Computer Brain) (4 CP base + 5 CP per point of capacity): A neural chip slot that allows the user to swap out specialized skill chips. (Example: A chip slot holding a 4-point skill costs 24 CP).
  • Digital Mind (5 CP): Consciousness running on an organic-synthetic substrate. Immune to biological telepathy and mind control, but vulnerable to digital hacking.
  • Mindlink (5 CP for 1 person, 10 CP for 2-9 people, 20 CP for 10-99 people): A secure, local wireless data network connecting you to specific individuals.
  • Intuitive Mathematician (5 CP): An integrated coprocessor performing lightning-fast calculations instantly.

These traits represent the vulnerabilities, design shortcuts, and societal consequences of abandoning biological purity.

Physical & Sensory Disadvantages

These are standalone disadvantages that yield bonus Character Points:

  • Electrical (-20 points): Internal cybernetic components are vulnerable to high-voltage surges. EMP and Ion attacks deal structural deactivation, potentially shutting down or damaging components.
  • Unhealing (Total) (-30 CP): Applies specifically to the HP and DR of fully cybernetic systems. They do not recover naturally; they must be physically repaired with tools and parts.
  • Unhealing (Partial) (-20 CP): Your organic body heals normally, but your cybernetic parts must be manually repaired.
  • Calibration Requirement (-5% to -10%): Hardware requires regular calibration. Requires an Armoury or Mechanic roll periodically to prevent system glitches. Typically -5% for monthly maintenance, and -10% for weekly/daily maintenance.
  • Numb (-20 CP): Common with budget prosthetics lacking sensory feedback loops. Character suffers a -3 penalty to tasks requiring fine motor skills or touch sensitivity in that limb.
  • Ham-Fisted (-5 or -10 CP): Common with heavy-duty construction limbs. Imposes a -3 (for -5 CP) or -6 (for -10 CP) penalty to manual dexterity tasks like picking locks, typing, or delicate wiring.
  • Susceptibility (Computer Viruses/Malware) (-1 to -4 CP / level): Neural implants are vulnerable to electronic warfare. Apply this level as a penalty to resist digital hacking or malware.
  • Unnatural Feature (-1 CP / level, max -5 CP): Glowing optics, noisy hydraulic joints, or chrome plating. Imposes an equivalent penalty to Disguise and attempts to blend into a crowd.

Social & Psychological Disadvantages

  • Addiction (Immuno-Suppressants) (-5 to -20 CP): The biological host body continuously attempts to reject the artificial implants. The character must regularly consume immuno-suppressant drugs or suffer severe physical deterioration.
  • Social Stigma (Cyborg/Minority) (-10 CP): In some sectors, heavily modified individuals are viewed as second-class citizens, suffering a -2 penalty on Reaction Rolls.
  • Social Stigma (Subjugated) (-20 CP): Classified as the legal property of a corporation or state military.
  • Secret (Illegal Tech) (-5 to -20 CP): Hiding restricted, military-grade combat implants or illegal black-market neural interfaces. Discovery leads to arrest or forcible extraction.
  • Debt (-1 CP per level of wealth owed): Deeply in debt to a megacorporation or loan shark for your hardware.
  • Duty (Corporate/Military) (-1 to -15 CP): You owe your life and your hardware to an organization. Mandatory, highly dangerous assignments when summoned.
  • Low Empathy (-20 CP): Neural processes have become highly logical and algorithmic. You suffer a -3 penalty to empathy-based social skills (Savoir-Faire, Diplomacy, Streetwise).
  • Callous (-5 CP): You have lost touch with your humanity. Imposes a -2 penalty to Teaching, Leadership, and Diplomacy.
  • Bloodlust (-10 CP): Combat programs override mercy parameters. You prefer to permanently neutralize threats.
  • Paranoia (-10 CP): Intense, systemic distrust. Convinced that hackers, corporate spies, or rivals are trying to compromise or sabotage your implants.

While droid-like replacement limbs are common for war veterans, the bleeding edge of enhancement lies in Neural Implants. Unlike standard prosthetics, neural implants interface directly with a user’s brain stem and central nervous system, altering biochemistry, amplifying reflexes, or pushing physical limits.

The Overlap Rule

You cannot have two implants installed that enhance the same attribute, secondary characteristic, or specific biological function at the same time. If an implant affects multiple attributes, it occupies the neural pathways for all of those attributes.

  • Example 1 (Safe): You install the Bavakar Strength System (+1 ST) and the Advanced Alacrity Implant (+1 DX). This is safe, as one routes to the muscular system and the other to the nervous system.
  • Example 2 (Conflict): You attempt to install the Bavakar Strength System (+1 ST) alongside the Cardio-Muscular Package (+2 ST, +1 HT). Because both devices attempt to override your Strength pathway, it causes immediate neural rejection.
  • Rejection Consequence: Attempting to install conflicting implants results in immediate neural overload, causing unconsciousness and 3d injury that bypasses DR. The conflicting implant is violently rejected and cannot be used until the other is uninstalled.

Neural Interface Chips: The physical component behind every Neural, Sensory, and Utility Implant below is a Silicon Interface Chip — the same order of magnitude as a Belt Circuit, and it works the same way: the firmware is flashed into it, not carried on a card left in a slot. A chip this small doesn't have room for its own card slot, so programming happens externally:

a blank Datacard (@UUID[Compendium.shadowbase.handbook.JournalEntry.Skjt6Gqhhw8BiF1Y]{Chapter 10}, 174 CR, 0.28 lb) is loaded with the implant's specific firmware at a Cybernetics Terminal -- the Dedicated Workshop (+0) tier for this trade, not a separate item to buy (see Programming a Datacard, @UUID[Compendium.shadowbase.handbook.JournalEntry.Skjt6Gqhhw8BiF1Y]{Chapter 10}) -- then flashed directly into the chip's onboard memory during Phase 3 (Firmware Calibration) of construction. Once flashed, the card's programming is spent and it reverts to a blank, reusable card — the Datacard is a construction tool here, not an installed part, so it never adds to the implant's final weight. This firmware Datacard is a separate card from the implant’s Blueprint (@UUID[Compendium.shadowbase.handbook.JournalEntry.Skjt6Gqhhw8BiF1Y]{Chapter 10}): building the implant needs both, and the firmware calibration (Phase 3, below) is part of the build.

Formula: an implant is priced from its component materials plus the value of what its firmware grants, run through the three Crafting Phases below.

Component Values: The component is the Silicon Interface Chip, at its material value; the firmware is worth 20 CR per CP of the granted benefit -- @UUID[Compendium.shadowbase.handbook.JournalEntry.Skjt6Gqhhw8BiF1Y]{Chapter 10}'s Traits Have a Price rate, the same one @UUID[Compendium.shadowbase.handbook.JournalEntry.sM4JaeipflPpOZgw]{Chapter 13} uses for belts and visors -- with multiple stacked traits summing their CP first.

Base Cost = (component value + 20 × CP) × 6, that ×6 being Phase 1 at ×3 (Physiology or Engineer (Cybernetics), both IQ/Hard) and Phase 2 at ×2 (Electronics Repair, IQ/Average).

Market Cost = Base Cost × 3, Phase 3 Neuro-Firmware Calibration at Computer Programming, IQ/Hard.

Exclusions: The blank Datacard is a construction tool rather than an installed part, as above, so its 174 CR never enters the total. Rows whose Notes state a different basis govern themselves -- see Crafting Phases, below.

These upgrades replace or enhance the body’s natural sensory organs and physiological systems, providing specialized tactical utility on the battlefield.

To prevent physical structural failure and sensory overload, installations are governed by two specific capacity rules:

The Anatomical Slot Rule (Sensory Implants)

Sensory implants are restricted by the natural biology of the user’s species. A standard human, for example, possesses two “Eye Slots” and two “Ear Slots.” You cannot install three cybernetic eyes unless your species naturally possesses three eyes.

  • Combinations: You may install a different upgrade in each available slot (e.g., Thermal in the left eye, Telescopic in the right), or you may combine multiple traits into a single cybernetic replacement (e.g., a single eye that has both Thermal and HUD capabilities) by paying the combined cost and weight. Combining traits significantly increases the surgical difficulty of the installation.

The Body Capacity Rule (Utility Implants)

Utility implants are housed within the body’s physical mass and are limited by available physical real estate. Each hit location has a maximum number of “Utility Slots”:

  • Torso: 2 Utility Slots
  • Head: 1 Utility Slot
  • Arms: 1 Utility Slot per arm
  • Legs: 1 Utility Slot per leg

If an implant occupies a Utility Slot in a specific location, another implant cannot be placed in that exact slot without removing the first one.

Crafting an implant is not the same operation as putting it into a patient. This section covers building the device on a bench; installing it is major invasive surgery with its own skill, cost, time and failure modes -- see Surgical Installation & Medical Risks, above. A finished implant is an inert object until a surgeon fits it, and a flawless fabrication roll does nothing to help a botched operation. Crafting neural and sensory implants is significantly more delicate than fabricating cybernetic limbs. While limbs require industrial shaping circuitry, and programming, implants demand sterile micro-fabrication and flawless neural mapping to avoid catastrophic brain rejection.

Building from a Blueprint: Every item you build -- in the tables above or not -- requires its Blueprint in hand (@UUID[Compendium.shadowbase.handbook.JournalEntry.Skjt6Gqhhw8BiF1Y]{Chapter 10}: Blueprints): buy it, reverse-engineer it from a Deconstruction, or author an original. A proven plan builds at the baseline; a degraded copy or an unproven original takes its penalty on every phase roll below.

Crafting Phases: An implant takes three phases, applied in order (@UUID[Compendium.shadowbase.handbook.JournalEntry.Skjt6Gqhhw8BiF1Y]{Chapter 10}'s Construction Markup).

  • Phase 1 is Biometric Mapping & Schematics, reading the host and turning that into a buildable spec; it needs Physiology to read the body or Engineer (Cybernetics) to draw the schematic, both IQ/Hard, so it multiplies by ×3.
  • Phase 2 is Micro-Hardware Fabrication and needs Electronics Repair (Cybernetics) or Electronics Repair (Medical), both IQ/Average, multiplying by ×2 -- the running total after this use is the implant's Base Cost.
  • Phase 3 is Neuro-Firmware Calibration and needs Computer Programming, IQ/Hard, multiplying by ×3 to give the Market Cost.

Surgical Installation: The fourth phase, Surgical Installation, is not a phase: it is work done on a patient rather than on the item, and its cost is the surgical fee, which is why the same implant is worth the same whoever ends up wearing it.

Scope: All three phases apply to Sensory and Utility Implants as much as to Neural ones -- Phase 1 is where a sensory implant is scaled to the host’s SM (see Material Scaling, below), so it is never skipped.

Exceptions: A row whose Notes state a different basis is the exception and governs itself -- Subdermal Armor Plating is priced as a standard physical component, ×2 to Base and ×2 again to Market, because it carries no chip and no firmware for Phases 1 and 3 to act on.

Phase 1: Biometric Mapping & Schematics Before micro-fabrication, the crafter must map the host’s specific neural pathways and determine material scaling.

  • Time: 4 hours for standard mapping.
  • Material Scaling:
  • Sensory & Utility Implants: Apply the SM weight multiplier formula to Base Material(s): Weight (Value) (a larger species requires larger cybernetic eyes or more subdermal plating).
  • Neural Implants: These interface directly with the brain stem or cortex. They do not scale with SM. A neural chip requires the same base material weight regardless of the host’s size.
  • Failure: A failed Engineer (Cybernetics) or Physiology roll results in flawed mapping. The crafter wastes 10% of the raw materials before catching the error and must re-roll this phase.

Phase 2: Micro-Hardware Fabrication The crafter constructs the microscopic logic gates, optic lenses, and delicate bio-silicon interface nodes.

  • Skills Required: Electronics Repair (Cybernetics) or Electronics Repair (Medical). Armoury and Machinist are too broad for this microscopic work.
  • Base Time: Fabrication takes 10 hours of continuous labor per 0.1 lbs. of the final item’s weight.
  • Workspace Modifiers:
  • Improvised/Field Tools (-5 to skill).
  • Basic Toolkit (-2 to skill).
  • Dedicated Cyber-Clinic (+0 to skill): Requires a clean-room environment.
  • Advanced Research Facility (+2 to skill).
  • Taking Extra Time: As @UUID[Compendium.shadowbase.handbook.JournalEntry.Skjt6Gqhhw8BiF1Y]{Chapter 10} (General Gear & Currency): double the base time for +1, four times for +2, eight times for +3, fifteen times for +4, thirty times for +5, whatever your tools.
  • Failure: A failed skill roll ruins the micro-circuitry. The crafter loses 50% of the raw materials and must restart this phase.

Phase 3: Neuro-Firmware Calibration The firmware must flawlessly translate digital signals into biological neurotransmitters.

Method A: Coding from Scratch

  • Skills Required: Computer Programming. Performed at a Cybernetics Terminal, the +0 workspace tier for this trade: load a blank Datacard (@UUID[Compendium.shadowbase.handbook.JournalEntry.Skjt6Gqhhw8BiF1Y]{Chapter 10}) with the target firmware, then flash it into the chip during this phase — the card reverts to blank once the flash succeeds.
  • Physiological Synergy: A successful Physiology (Neurology) or Bioengineering roll grants a +2 synergy bonus to the programming roll. An exceptional success halves total programming time.
  • Base Time: 1 hour of programming time per 100 Credits of the item's retail value. Read the item's Market Cost off its table and divide by 100 -- an Advanced Combat System at 12,780 CR takes 127.8 hours to code. The time follows the price, so if a price changes the time changes with it; never quote a fixed hour count for an item alongside a price that can move.
  • Failure: A failed Computer Programming roll creates a feedback loop. The crafter loses 25% of the invested time and must re-roll. A Critical Failure bricks the silicon components, requiring Phase 2 to be repeated for the processor.

Method B: Installing Salvaged Firmware If the crafter possesses a datacard containing intact firmware salvaged from an identical implant, they may completely bypass the manual coding process.

  • Skills Required: Computer Operation.
  • Base Time: 10 minutes of installation, diagnostics, and syncing.
  • Failure: A failed Computer Operation roll indicates a minor installation glitch or a biometric mismatch. The installer wastes 10 minutes and must attempt the roll again. A Critical Failure irreparably corrupts the software, wiping the datacard and forcing the crafter to revert to Method A to finish the implant.

Phase 4: Quality & Surgical Installation The lowest margin of success between Phase 2 and Phase 3 dictates the implant’s final quality. Two separate things resolve here, and they do not share a roll: the Failure entry belongs to the Surgery roll, while the Success margins grade the implant’s quality tier from the lowest margin between the Hardware (Phase 2) and Firmware (Phase 3) rolls. Because these implants interface directly with the brain or major sensory organs, the surgery is far more dangerous than attaching a limb.

  • Surgical Requirements: Takes 1d hours. Requires a Surgery roll, at -3 for Sensory/Utility implants, and -5 for Neural Implants. Spare parts and medical supplies equal to 20% of the base cost must be expended.
  • Failure: The implant functions but causes Neural Rejection. The user suffers a persistent -1 penalty to IQ or Will, and takes 2d injury that bypasses DR due to neural shock. A Critical Failure destroys the implant entirely, leaves the user comatose, and inflicts permanent brain or nerve damage (requiring advanced medical restoration).
  • Success (Margin 0-2): Standard Quality. Functions perfectly as listed.
  • Success (Margin 3-5): Fine Quality. Grants a +1 to HT rolls made to resist targeted electrical/ion disruption (EMP).
  • Success (Margin 6+ or Critical Success): Very Fine Quality. Integrates flawlessly, granting a +2 to HT rolls against EMPs, and the surgical recovery time for the host is halved.

pages.name: Swapping Firmware in an Installed Implant

text.content:
While the implant remains installed, its firmware can be replaced without pulling the physical Interface Chip or requiring surgery: load a blank Datacard with the new program and flash it through the implant's external port, exactly as a belt is reflashed (@UUID[Compendium.shadowbase.handbook.JournalEntry.sM4JaeipflPpOZgw]{Chapter 13}). The chip is a generic read/write target, not tied to any one firmware -- and no card stays in it — as noted under Firmware and Datacards above, there is no slot for one.

Skills Required: Computer Operation to flash the new program through the implant's external port.

Base Time: 10 minutes of syncing and biometric re-calibration.

Success: The implant now runs the new program; the old firmware is overwritten, and is gone unless it was read onto a card first. The Datacard used for the flash reverts to blank and is reused, exactly as after a fresh Crafting installation.

Failure: A minor installation glitch or biometric mismatch. The installer wastes 10 minutes and must attempt the roll again.

Critical Failure: The mismatch corrupts both the incoming and the chip’s prior calibration data. The implant is non-functional until a full Computer Programming roll re-establishes it, per Crafting.

text.content:
Removing an implant with the intent to reuse it, rather than melt it down, is slower and more careful work than a straight extraction -- the goal is a working Interface Chip ready for fresh firmware, not a pile of Silicon.

Skill: Electronics Repair (Cybernetics), or Surgery for a still-installed biological host.

Time: 3 hours of delicate micro-labor -- longer than a standard Salvage extraction, since the chip has to come out undamaged.

Success: The Interface Chip is extracted intact and ready to be flashed with new firmware for a different implant of the same size class, retaining its established Base Cost value (the Implants tables) for that purpose.

Critical Success: As above, and the extraction leaves no trace -- no HT roll or downtime needed for a biological host.

Failure: The chip cracks under removal; it’s only good for its Salvage raw-material yield (see above), not reuse.

Critical Failure: The chip is destroyed, and any lingering firmware triggers the same security-wipe/backlash consequences as a Critical Failure on the Logic Preservation roll (see Salvaging Neural and Sensory Implants, below).

While Salvaging reduces an implant straight to raw Silicon for a quick payout, Deconstruction recovers both of the things an implant is worth -- the Interface Chip itself, and the firmware flashed into it, which can be read back onto a blank Datacard prepared beforehand -- each usable in a different build rather than melted down.

Recording a Blueprint: A successful Deconstruction can also record a Blueprint of the implant (@UUID[Compendium.shadowbase.handbook.JournalEntry.Skjt6Gqhhw8BiF1Y]{Chapter 10}: Blueprints) -- a blank Datacard and a Computer Operation roll. Salvaging never yields one.

Skills Required: Electronics Repair (Cybernetics) to separate the chip from its housing without damage; Computer Programming to read the firmware off the chip onto a blank Datacard beforehand, if it is to be preserved rather than wiped.

Base Time: 2 hours of delicate micro-labor per component -- slower than Salvaging, in exchange for both pieces coming out usable instead of one blended material yield.

Success: The Interface Chip is recovered intact, ready to be flashed with new firmware, retaining its established Base Cost value (the Implants tables) for that purpose. If the firmware was read off first, it survives on the blank card that received it, reusable in a different implant of the same size class. Anything not extracted intact comes back as raw material separated by type, at 75% of its weight -- 90% on a critical success.

Critical Success: As above, plus 25% of the surrounding casing’s raw material weight is recovered too.

Failure: The chip cracks under separation; it's only good for Salvaging's raw-material yield, not reuse. Any firmware not read off beforehand is wiped with it.

Critical Failure: The chip is destroyed outright, and any lingering firmware triggers the same security-wipe/backlash consequences described under Crafting.

Extracting implants from a biological host or a destroyed chassis is a surgical and electronic puzzle. A heavy hand will permanently fracture the microscopic pathways.

Skills Required:

  • Biological Extraction: Surgery (to remove the implant from tissue without destroying the hardware).
  • Hardware Extraction (from destroyed droids/helmets): Electronics Repair (Cybernetics).
  • Data/Logic Preservation: Computer Programming (to stabilize the firmware during power-down).

Base Time:

  • Surgical/Hardware Extraction: 2 hours of delicate micro-labor.
  • Logic Preservation: 1 hour to safely unbind the firmware from the previous host’s biometric locks.

Yield Rates:

  • Standard Success: You recover 50% of the raw material weight (Silicon, Plastoid, Clari-crystalline).
  • Critical Success: You recover 75% of the raw material weight. If you prepared a blank datacard beforehand, you successfully download the neuro-firmware. This may be used in another part of the same type to bypass programming time.

Failure Conditions:

  • Extraction Failure: A failed Surgery or Electronics Repair roll cracks the casing and severs the interface pins. The implant is reduced to base scrap components (10% of base weight recovered).
  • Logic/Firmware Failure: A failed Computer Programming roll triggers a security wipe. The firmware is permanently corrupted, making the core processor useless, though raw materials can still be recovered.
  • Critical Failure: The implant’s micro-power cell ruptures or the bio-circuitry undergoes a catastrophic short. The salvager takes 1d-3 burn damage. If the implant was being surgically extracted from a living host, the host immediately suffers a Major Wound to the brain or corresponding sensory organ.

Workspace Modifiers & Taking Extra Time: Functions exactly as the rules outlined for cybernetic limbs. A clean, static-free environment is heavily encouraged to avoid rendering the silicon inert.

While Neural Implants enhance existing biology invisibly, the brutal nature of the Mandalorian Wars often necessitates full physical limb replacement. Replacing a limb does not take up a Neural Pathway, but it introduces its own set of structural benefits and vulnerabilities.

Extent of Replacement

Benefits, detriments, and upgrade capacities scale based on the size and scope of the replacement. Hands, feet, arms, and legs are purchased and upgraded as separate modular components. If a player wants to replace an entire leg, they must purchase both the Leg (Limb-Only) and the Foot (Partial) components.

  • Hand or Foot (Partial Replacement): Replaces the anatomy strictly from the wrist or ankle down. These can be attached to a natural biological limb or a cybernetic limb.
  • Upgrade Capacity: Can hold 1 Cybernetic Upgrade.
  • Power Cell: Charge lasts for 36 hours of use.
  • Arm or Leg (Full Replacement): Replaces the limb from the shoulder to the wrist, or from the hip to the ankle. Note: This does not* include the hand or foot, which must be purchased and calculated separately. Nothing stops a character fitting the limb alone -- but until the matching Hand or Foot is fitted, the prosthetic ends at the wrist or ankle, and the character has One Hand or One Foot (@UUID[Compendium.shadowbase.handbook.JournalEntry.LHqDwyGfdwXUdoZO]{Chapter 5}) for as long as it does. A character who cannot yet afford the extremity carries the disadvantage until they can.
  • Upgrade Capacity: Can hold up to 2 Cybernetic Upgrades.
  • Power Cell: Charge lasts for 72 hours of use.

Cybernetic Prosthetics

Because they are constructed from industrial metals, polymers, and synthetic weaves, cybernetic limbs provide innate Damage Resistance (DR). This innate cybernetic DR stacks with any worn armor on that location.

Bottom-Up Construction: prosthetics are built the same way as Armor Pieces (@UUID[Compendium.shadowbase.handbook.JournalEntry.sM4JaeipflPpOZgw]{Chapter 13}) — a Structural Chassis (Volume × Density, by material) plus a Neural Interface and Power Cell, with optional Enhancement Modules bolted on. the market price for a component is material value × 2, that ×2 being Phase 1, Armoury (Cybernetics) or Mechanic (Cybernetics) (both IQ/Average); the market price for the finished Chassis is that component price × 2 again (the same two-stage markup as Armor, Weapons, and Belts). Enhancement Modules price the same way, added directly to the total — they're small bolt-on parts, not full sub-assemblies, so they don't get marked up a second time.

Cybernetic Size Modifiers & Weights

Cybernetics are precision-fitted to function and balance properly, and must match a character’s Size Modifier (SM) exactly to be installed. All base weights and costs listed in the limb tables assume a standard SM 0 humanoid.

Characters who are larger or smaller must adjust the physical weight and the credit cost of their mechanical parts to reflect the amount of material and custom wiring used.

  • Static Components Exception: Static components built into the limb—most notably Power Cells—do not scale. Their cost and weight remain completely fixed regardless of the Size Modifier of the limb being constructed or resized.

To determine the final weight and cost of a cybernetic limb or implant for a non-standard size, find the character’s Size Modifier on the table below and multiply the SM 0 weight and cost by the listed factors.

Crafting Cybernetic Prosthetics

As with implants, building the limb and fitting it to a patient are two separate operations. This section covers fabrication only; attaching a prosthetic to a living body is surgery -- see Surgical Installation & Medical Risks, above -- and is paid for, rolled for, and can fail independently of how well the limb was made. Crafting a cybernetic limb from scratch requires a standard workspace equipped with metalworking, robotics, and cybernetic tools. The process is divided into distinct phases, accounting for the physical size of the wearer, hardware assembly, complex neural firmware, and the final surgical graft.

Building from a Blueprint: Every item you build -- whether it appears in this chapter’s tables or not -- requires its Blueprint in hand (@UUID[Compendium.shadowbase.handbook.JournalEntry.Skjt6Gqhhw8BiF1Y]{Chapter 10}: Blueprints): buy the plan for a catalog item, reverse-engineer it from a Deconstruction, or author an original through the Design Phase. Owning or knowing of an item is not knowing how to make one. A proven plan builds at the baseline; a degraded copy or an unproven original takes its penalty on every Crafting Phase roll below.

Crafting Phases: a prosthetic is priced from the finished components its Construction column lists, not from raw stock.

  • Their sum is the limb's Base Cost, and Market Cost = Base Cost × 2 -- that ×2 is Phase 2, Hardware Fabrication, an Average-tier phase (@UUID[Compendium.shadowbase.handbook.JournalEntry.Skjt6Gqhhw8BiF1Y]{Chapter 10}'s Construction Markup).
  • Phase 1, Sizing & Schematics, and Phase 3, Firmware Calibration, are not markups on the item: like Surgical Installation they are work done for a particular wearer -- scaling a standard SM 0 model to that body and calibrating firmware to that nervous system -- and are charged as a fee when the limb is fitted.

Catalog Pricing: This is why the same limb is worth the same whoever ends up wearing it, and why a listed model is a catalog product rather than a bespoke build. Implants price differently for exactly that reason: an implant is built from raw Silicon for one host, so its full ×3 × ×2 × ×3 chain sits in its price.

Phase 1: Sizing, Schematics, and Materials Before physical fabrication begins, the crafter must determine the material requirements based on the wearer’s Size Modifier (SM) and draft a schematic mapping the neural interfaces to the host’s specific biology.

Skills Required: Engineer (Cybernetics). This is the roll the Failure clause below refers to; a Blueprint's bonus applies to it as it does to every phase.

  • Time: 2 hours for a standard SM 0 build. Add 1 hour per +1 SM or per unique anatomical requirement (e.g., digitigrade legs, extra joints).
  • Material Scaling Formula: Apply the SM weight multiplier to the Base Material(s): Weight (Value) (excluding static components like Power Cells).
  • Final Material Amount = Base Material Weight x SM Multiplier Where:
  • Final Material Amount is the final required amount of a specific material for the target SM.
  • Base Material Weight is the explicit weight or unit quantity of that specific material listed in the SM 0 blueprint.
  • SM Multiplier is the scaling factor corresponding to the target Size Modifier.
  • Using the formula (Crafting an Athakam “Nimble-5” for a Dowutin) Example:*
  • Base Material Weight: The standard SM 0 blueprint for an Athakam “Nimble-5” requires 1.3 lbs of Plasteel, and 0.2 lbs of Silicon.
  • Target Size Modifier (SM): Dowutins are massive, towering aliens that fall under Size Modifier +2.
  • SM Multiplier: The scaling rules dictate that an SM +2 creature requires a multiplier of x2.
  • Adjusted Material: 2.6 lbs of Plasteel, and 0.4 lbs of Silicon.
  • Failure: A failed sizing and schematic roll using Engineer (Cybernetics) means flawed measurements. The crafter wastes 10% of the gathered raw materials before physical fabrication begins and must re-roll this phase.

Phase 2: Hardware Fabrication Once the scaling and materials are determined, the crafter must smelt and shape the chassis, weave the synthetic myomer musculature, lay the delicate neuro-circuitry, and safely integrate the static Power Cell.

  • Skills Required: Armoury (Cybernetics) or Mechanic (Cybernetics) for the chassis and myomer; Electronics Repair (Cybernetics) for circuitry and power integration.
  • Base Time: 1 hour of continuous labor per pound of the final scaled weight.
  • Workspace Modifiers:
  • Improvised/Field Tools (-5 to skill): Using pocket multi-tools and crude splicers.
  • Basic Toolkit (-2 to skill): Using portable electronics repair kits and a basic mechanic’s bay.
  • Dedicated Cyber-Clinic (+0 to skill): A facility specifically outfitted for cybernetic grafting and myomer weaving.
  • Advanced Research Facility (+2 to skill): Top-tier military cybernetics labs or corporate hospitals.
  • Taking Extra Time: As @UUID[Compendium.shadowbase.handbook.JournalEntry.Skjt6Gqhhw8BiF1Y]{Chapter 10} (General Gear & Currency): double the base time for +1, four times for +2, eight times for +3, fifteen times for +4, thirty times for +5, whatever your tools.
  • Failure: A failed skill roll ruins the circuitry pathways and completely drains the Power Cell. Both components must be replaced before the crafter can attempt this phase again. The physical casing is retained.

Phase 3: Firmware Calibration & Neural Interfacing The crafter must write and calibrate the proprietary code that translates the host’s central nervous system impulses into mechanical movement, matching the wearer’s specific biometric data.

Method A: Coding from Scratch

  • Skills Required: Computer Programming is mandatory. Performed at a Cybernetics Terminal, the +0 workspace tier for this trade: load a blank Datacard (@UUID[Compendium.shadowbase.handbook.JournalEntry.Skjt6Gqhhw8BiF1Y]{Chapter 10}) with the target firmware, then flash it into the chip during this phase — the card reverts to blank once the flash succeeds.
  • Physiological Synergy: A successful Physiology or Bioengineering roll grants a +2 synergy bonus to the Computer Programming roll. An exceptional success on the synergy roll halves the total required programming time.
  • Base Time: 1 hour of programming time per 100 Credits of the item’s retail value.
  • Failure: A failed Computer Programming roll indicates a severe latency bug. The crafter loses 25% of the invested time and must re-roll. A Critical Failure bricks the internal neuro-processors, requiring the Silicon to be entirely replaced and Phase 3 to start over.

Method B: Installing Salvaged Firmware If the crafter possesses a datacard containing intact firmware salvaged from an identical prosthetic, they may completely bypass the manual coding process.

  • Skills Required: Computer Operation.
  • Base Time: 10 minutes of installation, diagnostics, and syncing.
  • Failure: A failed Computer Operation roll indicates a minor installation glitch or a biometric mismatch. The installer wastes 10 minutes and must attempt the roll again. A Critical Failure irreparably corrupts the software, wiping the datacard and forcing the crafter to revert to Method A to finish the prosthetic.

Phase 4: Quality & Surgical Installation The lowest margin of success between the Hardware (Phase 2) and Firmware (Phase 3) rolls dictates the cybernetic’s final quality. Two separate things resolve here, and they do not share a roll. The Surgery roll below decides whether the installation succeeds at all -- its Failure and Critical Failure results are the ones listed under Failure. The quality tier is read off the lower of the Phase 2 and Phase 3 margins, and is what the three Success entries below grade. A limb can be Very Fine and still be installed badly, and a Standard one can go in flawlessly.

  • Surgical Requirements: Takes one full day and a Surgery roll. Spare parts and medical supplies equal to 20% of the target limb’s base cost must be expended. NPC clinic fees range from 20% to 50% of the limb’s final base value.
  • Failure: Produces a “buggy” limb. It functions but imposes a -1 penalty to DX for actions using that limb and causes 1d-3 toxic damage during installation from tissue rejection. A Critical Failure during Surgery halves the Innate DR, renders the limb non-functional, and causes 1d damage with severe localized infection.
  • Success (Margin 0-2): Standard Quality. Provides full Innate DR and functions perfectly.
  • Success (Margin 3-5): Fine Quality. Grants a minor benefit: +1 to physical breakage resistance, 10% weight reduction, or a +1 to HT rolls made to resist targeted electrical/ion disruption.
  • Success (Margin 6+ or Critical Success): Very Fine Quality. A masterwork piece integrating seamlessly with the host.

Swapping Enhancement Modules

While the limb remains attached to its host, an installed Enhancement Module (Myomer Boost, Cortosis Plating, or similar) can be replaced with a different one without fully detaching the limb -- the module bay is accessible without a full Uninstall.

Skills Required: Armoury (Cybernetics) or Mechanic (Cybernetics).

Base Time: 30 minutes per module swapped.

Success: The old module is removed intact and the new one seated correctly, retaining its established Base Cost value (the Enhancement Modules table) if resold or reused elsewhere.

Failure: The new module is improperly seated. The limb is non-functional until another 30 minutes of work.

Critical Failure: The mounting rail is damaged, disabling that module slot until a successful repair roll restores it.

Swapping Prosthetic Components

Replacing a Prosthetic Component -- the Chassis itself, or a component seated in it -- while the limb stays attached to its host. Distinct from Swapping Enhancement Modules, which reaches only the module bay, and from Uninstalling, which detaches the whole limb. Because the work reaches structure the host's nerves are spliced into, this is a surgical procedure: it needs a sterile environment and the surgeon's roll, not a bench.

Skills Required: Surgery, plus Armoury (Cybernetics) or Mechanic (Cybernetics) for the hardware. Base Time: 1 hour per component swapped. Surgical Cost: half the usual installation fee, since the limb is not being detached. Success: the old component comes out intact at its established value and the new one seats cleanly. Failure: the component is seated badly -- the limb functions but the swapped component's bonuses stay offline until a successful recalibration. Critical Failure: the component is ruined, yielding 25% of its raw material weight, and the host takes 1d damage to the limb's location.

Uninstalling Cybernetic Prosthetics

Removing a whole prosthetic limb intact -- to fit it on a different host, sell it as a working unit, or store it -- is a more careful, deliberate process than salvaging it for raw materials, and preserves the chassis, myomer musculature, and neural circuitry as reusable components rather than reducing them to scrap.

Skills Required: Surgery or Armoury (Cybernetics) for the physical detachment; Electronics Repair (Cybernetics) to safely disconnect the neural interface without corrupting its firmware.

Base Time: 2 hours of surgery per limb (Hand/Foot), or 4 hours per limb (Arm/Leg).

Success: The limb is removed with its chassis, musculature, and neural circuitry fully intact, retaining its established Base Cost value (the Named Prosthetics table, or the appropriate Chassis/Component catalog) if installed on a new host or resold as a working unit.

Failure: The detachment is clumsy. The limb is removed but is now “Broken” (see Item Condition and Degradation, below) and requires repair before it can be installed on a new host.

Critical Failure: A catastrophic error during detachment destroys the neural circuitry beyond repair. The limb can still be removed, but only its Salvage raw-material yield can be recovered from it -- it can no longer function as a prosthetic.

Deconstructing Cybernetic Prosthetics

While Salvaging reduces a prosthetic limb straight to raw materials for a quick payout, Deconstruction separates it into its constituent components -- the Chassis, the Neural Interface, the Power Cell, and any installed Enhancement Modules -- each recovered intact and ready to mount into a different build, rather than melted down. Exactly the same logic as Deconstructing an Armor Piece (@UUID[Compendium.shadowbase.handbook.JournalEntry.sM4JaeipflPpOZgw]{Chapter 13}): the Chassis and any installed Enhancement Module come apart as separate, reusable, intact components instead of being reduced to scrap. Ideal for stripping a captured Mandalorian-Forged limb to remount its Beskar Chassis on a custom build.

Recording a Blueprint: A successful Deconstruction is also the moment to record a Blueprint of the prosthetic (@UUID[Compendium.shadowbase.handbook.JournalEntry.Skjt6Gqhhw8BiF1Y]{Chapter 10}: Blueprints) -- a blank Datacard and a Computer Operation roll, made during the teardown. Salvaging never yields one.

Skills Required: Machinist or Armoury (Cybernetics) for the Chassis; Electronics Repair (Cybernetics) for the Neural Interface and any Enhancement Modules.

Base Time: 45 minutes of labor per pound of total weight -- between Crafting’s full hour of assembly and Salvaging’s half hour of teardown.

Success: Extract one intact, reusable component of the crafter’s choice (the Chassis, the Neural Interface, or a specific Enhancement Module), each retaining its own established Base Cost value (the Prosthetic Chassis, Prosthetic Components, and Enhancement Modules tables) when used in a new build.

Critical Success: Flawless teardown -- every component making up the limb is extracted fully intact and reusable, including the Power Cell.

Failure: The targeted component is ruined; the rest of the limb reduces to Salvaging’s raw-material yield instead.

Critical Failure: The limb is destroyed outright; 1d-3 damage to the crafter if the Chassis was Beskar or Phrik (residual stress discharge).

Salvaging Cybernetic Prosthetics

When you recover damaged, obsolete, or scavenged cybernetic limbs, you can dismantle them to reclaim expensive raw materials, synth-myomer muscle fibers, and intact neural processors.

Skills Required:

  • Chassis & Structural Components: Machinist or Armoury (Cybernetics).
  • Myomer Musculature: Mechanic (Cybernetics) or Physiology.
  • Neural Circuitry: Electronics Repair (Cybernetics) or Computer Programming.

Base Time:

  • Salvaging: 30 minutes of labor per pound of total weight.
  • Neural Processor Extraction: 60 minutes of extremely precise, high-risk work to remove the proprietary neural interface chips without damaging the firmware or the surrounding logic gates.

Yield Rates:

  • Standard Success: You recover 50% of the raw material weight (Silicon, Plastoid, Durasteel, etc.).
  • Critical Success: You recover 75% of the raw material weight. If you prepared a blank datacard beforehand, you successfully download the cybernetic’s firmware. This may be used in another part of the same type to reduce programming time by 50%.

Failure Conditions:

  • Structural Failure: A failed Machinist or Armoury roll results in the chassis being cracked or the mounting points sheared. The raw materials are reduced to “Scrap Metal” quality and cannot be used for high-tier crafting without significant purification.
  • Neural/Logic Failure: A failed Electronics Repair or Computer Programming roll causes a surge during the delicate removal of the neural processor. The processor unit is “bricked” and rendered useless, and the internal myomer fibers are fused into the chassis, making them unrecoverable.
  • Critical Failure: A catastrophic error occurs. The power cell or backup battery shorts out, causing a violent spark or chemical fire. No materials are recovered, and the salvager suffers 1d-3 burn damage and 1d-3 crushing damage from the resulting explosion.

Workspace Modifiers:

  • Improvised/Field Tools (-5 to skill): Trying to pick apart hardened cybernetic casing with basic hand tools.
  • Basic Toolkit (-2 to skill): Standard field-repair kit in a cluttered or unstable environment.
  • Dedicated Cyber-Clinic (+0 to skill): A proper workshop with a stable power supply and static-free surfaces.
  • Advanced Research Facility (+2 to skill): High-tier military lab or corporate medical bay equipped with diagnostic scanners that assist in locating fragile internal components.

Taking Extra Time: As @UUID[Compendium.shadowbase.handbook.JournalEntry.Skjt6Gqhhw8BiF1Y]{Chapter 10} (General Gear & Currency): double the base time for +1, four times for +2, eight times for +3, fifteen times for +4, thirty times for +5, whatever your tools.

Prosthetic Resizing

When adjusting a scavenged or off-the-shelf cybernetic limb to fit a different SM, the technician must undergo a rigorous modification process to alter the existing chassis.

Phase 1: Modification Blueprinting Before physical alterations begin, the technician must draft a schematic to map out how the pre-existing mechanical limb will be extended or contracted to fit the host.

  • Requirements: Takes 1d hours of focused work and requires a successful Engineer (Cybernetics) roll.
  • Modifiers: Apply a -2 penalty if scaling the cybernetic to a non-standard Size Modifier. Apply a -1 penalty per Cybernetic Upgrade being integrated.
  • Failure: The blueprint must be scrapped and redrawn, requiring another 1d hours and a new skill roll.
  • Critical Failure: The blueprint contains a catastrophic hidden error. The subsequent Surgery roll to install the limb will be made at an additional -4 penalty, and any standard failure becomes a Critical Failure.

Phase 2: Material Resizing & Alteration With a viable blueprint, the technician must physically alter the chassis, extend the myomer musculature, and splice additional synthetic nerve analogs.

  • Calculating Material Needed: Calculate the difference in weight between the cybernetic at its current SM and the target SM. This dictates exactly how much raw material must be purchased or scavenged, divided proportionally among the declared materials for that item (e.g., Durasteel, Silicon, Cortosis).
  • Fabrication Check: Requires an Armoury (Cybernetics) or Mechanic (Cybernetics) roll and one full day of labor. Success means the limb is physically prepped.

Phase 3: Surgical Grafting Surgical installation follows the same rules as Phase 4 of crafting. Resizing and installing a cybernetic in the field without professional medical facilities carries significant risk. It takes one full day, requiring the aforementioned Armoury/Mechanic roll to physically resize the limb, followed immediately by a Surgery roll.

Damage, Degradation, HP Penetration, & Repair

Cybernetic limbs rely on their DR to represent their structural integrity. They protect the host’s HP, but degrade under heavy fire.

  • HP Damage (Penetration): Resolve damage normally against the limb’s current DR. Any damage exceeding the limb’s DR penetrates to the character’s HP.
  • Deterioration: For every full 5 points of basic damage an attack rolls against that location (before subtracting DR), the cybernetic’s innate DR drops permanently by 1 point.
  • Destruction (DR 0): If a cybernetic’s innate DR reaches 0, the part is broken, and if another hit is landed on it, it becomes completely destroyed. A broken, or destroyed leg causes the character to fall prone; a broken, or destroyed arm drops whatever it was holding. Further attacks bypass DR completely.
  • Modular Replacement: Extremities and main limbs track DR independently. If a hand is broken, or destroyed, the main arm remains unaffected and only the hand needs replacing.
  • Repairs: Restoring 1 point of lost DR takes 2 hours of work, a successful Mechanic (Cybernetics) or Armoury (Cybernetics) roll, and spare parts equal to 10% of the limb’s base cost. A limb at 0 DR cannot be repaired.

Crafting Prosthetic Upgrades

Building a prosthetic upgrade -- a hidden compartment, a built-in tool, or a mounted device -- is a separate process from installing it into an existing limb (see Installing Prosthetic Upgrades, below). The upgrade must exist as a finished, self-contained unit before a technician can graft it in.

Building from a Blueprint: Every item you build -- in the tables above or not -- requires its Blueprint in hand (@UUID[Compendium.shadowbase.handbook.JournalEntry.Skjt6Gqhhw8BiF1Y]{Chapter 10}: Blueprints): buy it, reverse-engineer it from a Deconstruction, or author an original. A proven plan builds at the baseline; a degraded copy or an unproven original takes its penalty on every phase roll below.

Phase 1: Housing & Mounting Fabrication The technician carves, shapes, or machines the physical housing, cavity, or mounting bracket that will hold the upgrade -- a hollow compartment, a weapon mount, or a sensor housing.

Skills Required: Machinist or Armoury (Cybernetics).

Base Time: 2 hours of focused work per upgrade slot.

Failure: The housing is malformed or structurally unsound. The technician wastes 25% of the raw materials and must re-roll this phase. A Critical Failure ruins the materials entirely and cracks the surrounding chassis, requiring a separate Machinist or Armoury (Cybernetics) repair roll before work can continue.

Phase 2: Electronics & Programming (if applicable) Upgrades with functional electronics -- a Scomp Link Interface, Magnetic Grip (Cybernetic), or similar -- require this phase in addition to Phase 1. Purely physical upgrades (a Smuggler’s Compartment, a weapon mount for Concealed Weaponry) skip this phase entirely.

Skills Required: Electronics Repair (Cybernetics) for the circuitry, then Computer Programming to calibrate any sensor or skill-assist functions -- the same Computer Programming requirement already noted on affected items above.

Base Time: 3 hours of labor and calibration per upgrade slot.

Failure: A failed Electronics Repair roll ruins the circuitry (50% of raw materials lost, re-roll this phase). A failed Computer Programming roll leaves the upgrade physically complete but non-functional until a new programming roll is made; this does not require rebuilding the hardware.

Installing Prosthetic Upgrades

Installing a cybernetic upgrade requires a sterile environment and the precision to weave synthetic nerves into the host’s existing neural network. A botched installation can lead to “ghost pain,” motor-latency, or total rejection of the prosthetic.

Skills Required

  • Physical Hardware: Armoury (Cybernetics) or Mechanic (Cybernetics) is required for structural mounting.
  • Neural & Power Integration: Electronics Repair (Cybernetics) is the primary skill for syncing neural pins and power distribution.
  • Software Tuning: Computer Programming (mandatory for non-salvaged firmware) or Electronics Operation (if using pre-calibrated firmware) to sync the limb to the user’s biometrics.

Base Time & Workspace

  • Hardware/Neural Graft: 2 hours of delicate surgery/labor per upgrade slot.
  • Software Tuning: 1 hour of neural handshake testing and biometric synchronization.
  • Workspace Modifiers:
  • Improvised/Field Tools: -5 to skill.
  • Basic Toolkit: -2 to skill.
  • Dedicated Cyber-Clinic: +0 to skill.
  • Advanced Research Facility: +2 to skill.

Failure Consequences

  • Physical/Neural Failures:
  • Standard Failure: The interface is misaligned, causing phantom inputs or “dropped” signals. The upgrade is non-functional; the installer must spend 1 hour recalibrating the neural pins.
  • Critical Failure: The implant shorts out, causing 1d-3 toxic damage to the character from localized neural shock. The upgrade is ruined and the host limb suffers a -1 DX penalty until successfully repaired.
  • Software/Tuning Failures:
  • Standard Failure: The limb is physically sound, but the firmware refuses to sync. The software is unresponsive; the installer must spend 30 minutes debugging and attempt the roll again.
  • Critical Failure: The firmware enters a feedback loop. The upgrade is bricked, and the user suffers -2 to all DX-based rolls involving that limb until a Computer Programming or Electronics Repair (Cybernetics) roll is made to purge the faulty software.

Uninstalling Prosthetic Upgrades

Extraction of a high-end upgrade, such as a Mandalorian-forged interface or an Echani sensory suite, is a surgical process. Removing a “locked-in” component without damaging the host limb is a high-risk task.

Skills Required

  • Surgical Extraction: Surgery or Armoury (Cybernetics).

Base Time

  • 1 hour of surgery per upgrade slot.

Success Conditions

  • Standard Success: The component is removed with its full integrity intact.
  • Standard Failure: The mounting brackets are warped or a nerve-analog is severed. The component is removed but is now “Broken.” It requires a successful Repair roll (at -2) before it can be installed in a new limb.
  • Critical Failure: A catastrophic error occurs during extraction (e.g., the power cell shorts or a neural pin fuses). The upgrade is destroyed, and the host limb suffers a -2 HT penalty due to nerve damage until an Armoury (Cybernetics) repair roll is made.

Deconstructing Prosthetic Upgrades

While Salvaging melts an upgrade down to one blended raw-material yield, Deconstruction recovers each distinct material separately at a better rate -- and for upgrades with functional electronics (a Scomp Link Interface, Magnetic Grip (Cybernetic), or similar), preserves the programmed firmware intact instead of wiping it, provided a blank Datacard was prepared beforehand.

Recording a Blueprint: A successful Deconstruction can also record a Blueprint of the upgrade (@UUID[Compendium.shadowbase.handbook.JournalEntry.Skjt6Gqhhw8BiF1Y]{Chapter 10}: Blueprints) -- a blank Datacard and a Computer Operation roll. Salvaging never yields one.

Skills Required: Machinist for the housing; Electronics Repair (Cybernetics) for any functional circuitry; Computer Programming to preserve firmware rather than wipe it.

Base Time: 30 minutes of labor per pound of the upgrade’s total weight -- twice Salvaging’s time, in exchange for material-by-material precision.

Success: Recover 50% of each distinct material’s raw weight, separately, rather than one blended total.

Critical Success: 75% of each material, and if a blank Datacard was prepared beforehand, any programmed firmware is preserved intact instead of being wiped.

Failure: The same consequences as Salvaging, above -- the attempt is still a delicate teardown, just aimed at precision instead of speed.

Salvaging Prosthetic Upgrades

When you recover a damaged, obsolete, or uninstalled prosthetic upgrade, you can dismantle it to reclaim raw materials rather than repair or reuse it whole.

Skills Required: Housing & Mounting: Machinist or Armoury (Cybernetics). Electronics (if present): Electronics Repair (Cybernetics) for upgrades with functional circuitry, such as a Scomp Link Interface or Magnetic Grip (Cybernetic).

Base Time: 15 minutes of labor per pound of the upgrade’s total weight.

Yield Rates: Standard Success: You recover 50% of the raw material weight (Durasteel, Silicon, etc.). Critical Success: You recover 75% of the raw material weight.

Failure Conditions: Structural Failure: A failed Machinist or Armoury roll reduces the raw materials to “Scrap Metal” quality, unusable for anything requiring a specific named material. Electronic Failure: A failed Electronics Repair roll destroys the circuitry entirely; no materials are recovered from that portion of the upgrade. Critical Failure: The upgrade’s materials are ruined outright, and if it still held a charged Power Cell, the salvager suffers 1d-3 burn damage from a violent short.

Workspace Modifiers: Follows the same Improvised/Field Tools (-5), Basic Toolkit (-2), Dedicated Cyber-Clinic (+0), and Advanced Research Facility (+2) modifiers used throughout this chapter.

In the harsh environments of the Outer Rim and the relentless battles of the Mandalorian Wars, equipment degrades under stress, plasma scoring, and kinetic impact. To streamline tracking gear health without monitoring individual Hit Points for every item, all weapons, armor, belts, and utility gear utilize a universal four-step condition tracker governed by their Durability (Dur) rating.

Dur represents the overall structural health of a weapon category (Axe, Sword, Blaster, Gauntlet, etc.). During combat, exceeding this threshold degrades the item’s condition.

The Four Condition States The transition between states happens automatically when an item’s Durability threshold is breached in combat (see @UUID[Compendium.shadowbase.handbook.JournalEntry.JJ04T5LHImjlILs1]{Chapter 7} for Combat Damage Thresholds).

  • Fine: The item is in optimal condition. It functions exactly as written at its baseline statistics.
  • Damaged: The item has suffered structural stress, overheating, or component misalignment. A weapon's Malfunction range widens as its Durability falls -- see Malfunctions (Malf), @UUID[Compendium.shadowbase.handbook.JournalEntry.JJ04T5LHImjlILs1]{Chapter 7}, for the graduated thresholds. Armor and Shields have their DR reduced as described there.
  • Broken: The item is completely inoperable and requires significant overhaul. Weapons cannot fire, strike, or parry. Armor provides 0 DR, and environmental seals fail. Utility devices deactivate instantly.
  • Destroyed (Scrap): The item’s structural integrity or delicate internal circuitry is permanently ruined. It can never be repaired and is stripped of all modification slots. It can only be broken down for raw materials using standard salvaging rules.

Maintenance and Field Repairs Characters can utilize their technical skills to maintain their loadouts outside of active combat.

  • Field Repairs (Damaged to Fine): Characters can use the Armoury or Mechanic skill to “clean” and mend a Damaged item. This requires 10 minutes of uninterrupted work per item. If they succeed by a margin of 3+, the item is restored to Fine condition.
  • Overhauls (Broken or Destroyed): If an item is Broken or Destroyed, it can no longer be repaired in the field—it must be brought to a dedicated workshop or broken down for parts.
